title: Data Tables and Charts
learningGoals: Extract specific values from a multi-row, multi-column table
Find the row or column with the maximum or minimum total
Calculate an average from a row or column of data
Read bar charts and identify the tallest and shortest bars
Interpret pie chart sectors as percentages and absolute values
Describe whether a line graph shows an increasing, decreasing, or fluctuating trend
coreIdeas: Always scan the whole table before answering — never assume which row is largest without adding all values
Average = Total sum divided by number of items
In a bar chart, bar height equals value; a taller bar means a higher value
Pie chart actual count = (percentage divided by 100) multiplied by total
A sector less than 25% of a pie is smaller than one quarter of the whole
Line graph trend: values generally going up = increasing; generally going down = decreasing; up and down alternately = fluctuating

workedExamples.problem: Class A: Math=85, Sci=78, Eng=90, SS=72. Class B: Math=92, Sci=80, Eng=85, SS=88. Class C: Math=78, Sci=72, Eng=69, SS=80. Which class has the highest total?
workedExamples.solution: Class A total = 85+78+90+72 = 325. Class B total = 92+80+85+88 = 345. Class C total = 78+72+69+80 = 299. Class B has the highest total (345).
workedExamples.concept: Reading a table — finding the row with the maximum sum

workedExamples.problem: Class A scores: Math=85, Sci=78, Eng=90, SS=72. Find the average score.
workedExamples.concept: Calculating average from a table row

workedExamples.problem: A pie chart has 4 sectors: 30%, 25%, 25%, 20%. Total students = 200. How many students are in the 30% sector?
workedExamples.concept: Pie chart — converting percentage to absolute count

workedExamples.problem: Line graph values for Jan through Jun: 20, 25, 30, 28, 35, 40. Describe the trend.
workedExamples.solution: Values generally increase from 20 to 40 over 6 months with one small dip in April. The trend is mostly increasing.

workedExamples.problem: A bar chart shows 5 student scores: 45, 72, 68, 90, 55. How many more marks does the topper have than the lowest scorer?
workedExamples.concept: Bar chart — finding difference between maximum and minimum

onboarding.hook: Numbers in a table or chart can tell you the whole story — if you know which question to ask!
onboarding.avatarIntro: Hey! I am Spark. Data Interpretation is the skill of reading organised information quickly and answering questions accurately. Today we work with tables, bar charts, pie charts, and line graphs — all four types!
onboarding.priorKnowledge: You have already added and divided numbers. Today we apply those skills to real data arranged in charts and tables, just like you will see in aptitude tests.

duolingoLessonArc.mission: Complete 9 exercise groups across all four chart types and earn the Data Detective badge.
duolingoLessonArc.microLessonPattern: Show the chart → Ask a question → Identify the relevant data → Calculate → Instant Feedback
duolingoLessonArc.rewardLoop: 10 XP per correct answer; showing working before the answer earns 5 bonus XP.
duolingoLessonArc.reviewLoop: After group E, a flash review picks one question from groups A through D to reinforce table and bar chart skills.

uiDirectives.boardStyle: grid table or ASCII chart representation with labelled axes
uiDirectives.inputType: numeric input or multiple choice (4 options)

sessionFlow.coachHook: Scan the table, add the rows, find the champion!

boardDemo.title: Classes A, B, C with 4 subjects each. Find the class with highest total.
steps: Class B has the highest total: 345
boardDemo.teacherLine: Never eyeball a table and guess. Always add the rows completely. Class B wins with 345.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Add each row completely. Class A = 325, Class B = 345, Class C = 299. Highest total: Class B.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Using the same table, which class has the LOWEST total?  (a) Class A  (b) Class B  (c) Class C  (d) All equal
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Class C total = 299 — the lowest among the three classes.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Class C: 78+72+69+80 = 299. That is the smallest of the three totals.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: By how many marks does Class B outscore Class C?

sessionFlow.coachHook: Average = Total divided by number of subjects. Simple but powerful!

boardDemo.title: Class A: 85, 78, 90, 72 — Find the average score.
boardDemo.teacherLine: Divide the row total by the number of values. If it does not divide evenly, round to the nearest whole number.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Average for Class A = 325 divided by 4 = 81.25, approximately 81.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Class C scores: 78, 72, 69, 80. Find the average (round to nearest whole number).  (a) 74  (b) 75  (c) 73  (d) 76
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Well done! 299 divided by 4 = 74.75, which rounds to 75. Average calculation nailed!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Total = 78+72+69+80 = 299. Average = 299 divided by 4 = 74.75, which rounds to 75.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Which class has the highest average — A, B, or C? Show your working.

sessionFlow.coachHook: In a bar chart, taller bar = bigger value. Find the peak!

boardDemo.title: Bar chart: 5 students' scores — Student A=45, B=72, C=68, D=90, E=55
steps: The tallest bar belongs to Student D (score = 90)
Answer: Student D has the highest score
boardDemo.teacherLine: Scan the bars visually for the tallest, but always confirm by reading the exact value on the axis.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Bar chart shows 5 bars. Tallest bar = Student D = 90 marks.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: From the same bar chart (A=45, B=72, C=68, D=90, E=55), which student scored the LOWEST?  (a) Student A  (b) Student B  (c) Student C  (d) Student E
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Student A scored 45 — the lowest bar on the chart.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The shortest bar is Student A with a score of 45.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: List the five students in order from lowest to highest score.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Bar Chart — Difference Between Two Bars
sessionFlow.coachHook: Two bars, two values — how far apart are they?

boardDemo.title: Topper (Student D = 90) vs Lowest (Student A = 45). Find the difference.
steps: Identify the two bars: D = 90, A = 45
Student D scored 45 marks more than Student A
boardDemo.teacherLine: Always read both values carefully from the axis before subtracting. Estimation alone causes errors.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Difference = Highest score − Lowest score = 90 − 45 = 45 marks.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Student B scored 72. Student E scored 55. How many more marks did B score than E?  (a) 17  (b) 15  (c) 18  (d) 12
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! 72 − 55 = 17. You are reading bar charts accurately!
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: What is the difference between the second highest and second lowest scorer?

sessionFlow.subtopic: Pie Chart — Converting Percentage to Count
sessionFlow.coachHook: A pie chart slice's size tells you its share. Convert that share into actual numbers!

boardDemo.title: Pie chart: 4 sectors — 30%, 25%, 25%, 20%. Total = 200 students. Find count in 30% sector.
boardDemo.teacherLine: Percentage means per 100. So 30% of 200 means 30 out of every 100, times 2 groups of 100 = 60.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Count = percentage multiplied by total divided by 100 = 30 multiplied by 200 divided by 100 = 60.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Same pie chart. Total = 200. How many students are in the 25% sector?  (a) 40  (b) 50  (c) 55  (d) 25
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! 25% of 200 = 25 multiplied by 200 divided by 100 = 50 students.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Verify that all four sector counts add to 200 (sectors: 30%, 25%, 25%, 20%).

sessionFlow.subtopic: Pie Chart — Identifying the Smallest Sector
sessionFlow.coachHook: Which slice is smaller than one quarter? Think: one quarter = 25%!

boardDemo.title: Pie chart sectors: 30%, 25%, 25%, 20%. Which sector is less than 1/4 of the whole?
steps: Only the 20% sector is less than one quarter
boardDemo.teacherLine: One quarter = 25%. Any sector with a percentage below 25% is smaller than a quarter of the pie.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: One quarter = 25%. The 20% sector is the only one below 25%, so it is less than one quarter.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: A pie chart has sectors: 40%, 35%, 15%, 10%. Which sectors are less than 1/4 (25%)?  (a) 40% and 35%  (b) 15% only  (c) 15% and 10%  (d) 10% only
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Both 15% and 10% are less than 25% (one quarter). Well spotted!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: One quarter = 25%. Any sector below 25% qualifies: both 15% and 10% are below 25%.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: If a pie chart has a sector of exactly 25%, does it represent less than, equal to, or more than one quarter?

sessionFlow.coachHook: A line graph tells a story over time. Is it going up, down, or both?

boardDemo.title: Monthly values Jan to Jun: 20, 25, 30, 28, 35, 40. Describe the trend.
steps: Plot values: Jan=20, Feb=25, Mar=30, Apr=28, May=35, Jun=40
Check each step: up, up, up, small dip, up, up
Overall: from 20 to 40 with one small dip in April
boardDemo.teacherLine: A single dip does not reverse the overall trend. Look at the start and end values — from 20 to 40, the overall direction is clearly upward.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Start = 20, End = 40. One dip in April. Overall trend = mostly increasing.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Line graph values: 50, 45, 40, 38, 35, 30. What is the trend?  (a) Increasing  (b) Decreasing  (c) Constant  (d) Fluctuating
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! From 50 down to 30 — a clear decreasing trend.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Each value is smaller than the previous: 50, 45, 40, 38, 35, 30. That is a decreasing trend.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Give a real-life example of something that might show a decreasing line graph over 6 months.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Combined Data Interpretation — Two Questions, One Chart
sessionFlow.coachHook: One chart, two questions — read it once, answer both!

boardDemo.title: Bar chart: A=45, B=72, C=68, D=90, E=55. Find (1) max value and (2) difference between B and E.
steps: Question 1: Max value = highest bar = D = 90
Both answers from one reading of the chart
boardDemo.teacherLine: In exam DI sets, multiple questions share the same chart. Read all questions first, then scan the chart once for all answers — saves time!

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Max = D = 90. Difference B and E = 72 − 55 = 17. Two answers, one chart scan.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Same bar chart. What is the sum of the two lowest scorers (A and E)?  (a) 100  (b) 95  (c) 90  (d) 105
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Identify the two lowest bars: A=45 and E=55. Sum = 45+55 = 100.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: How many students scored above the overall average (average of all 5 students)?

sessionFlow.subtopic: Speed Round — One Question Per Chart Type
sessionFlow.coachHook: Final round! One question each from table, bar chart, pie chart, and line graph. Maximum focus!

boardDemo.title: Speed DI Strategy
steps: Bar chart: read the axis, compare heights
Pie chart: multiply percentage by total, divide by 100
Line graph: compare first and last value for trend
boardDemo.teacherLine: Identify the chart type in 4 seconds, extract key numbers in 10 seconds, calculate in 5 seconds. That is the 4-10-5 DI method.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Identify chart type, extract numbers, calculate — in that order.
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: A pie chart shows 4 sectors: 40%, 30%, 20%, 10%. Total = 500. How many are in the 10% sector?  (a) 50  (b) 100  (c) 40  (d) 10
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Perfect! 10% of 500 = 50. Speed round complete — you are a Data Detective!
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Name all four chart types covered today and one key question you can answer from each.

beats.teacherLine: Imagine the school announces the top-scoring class in exams — but the data is a messy table. Who won? You need Data Interpretation skills to find out in 30 seconds. That is exactly what we practice today!
boardSteps: Display a 3x4 table of class marks
Ask: Which class is the winner?
Prompt student to add each row

beats.teacherLine: There are four data formats today: tables (you add and compare), bar charts (you compare heights), pie charts (you convert percentage to count), and line graphs (you describe the trend). Different formats, same skill — extract the right numbers and calculate.
boardSteps: Show one example of each chart type
Label the key feature of each
Write the core calculation for each type

beats.teacherLine: Pie chart question: a school has 300 students. 25% are in the Science club. How many students is that? Think: percentage multiplied by total divided by 100.
boardSteps: Draw a pie chart with a 25% sector highlighted
Student writes: 25 multiplied by 300 divided by 100

beats.teacherLine: Data Interpretation is not about maths alone — it is about reading carefully and calculating accurately. Remember the four types: table, bar, pie, line. You have earned the Data Detective badge today!
boardSteps: Show summary: 4 chart types with one key rule each
